props.title: Performance
props.initialSlug: Gangster hides with rock star, identities unravel

sections.content: Performance (1970) revolutionized British cinema by smashing together London's criminal underworld with its psychedelic counterculture. Directors Donald Cammell and Nicolas Roeg created a hallucinatory masterpiece where James Fox's gangster Chas crashes into Mick Jagger's reclusive rock star Turner. The film's fragmented editing style, sexual fluidity, and identity-melding narrative influenced everything from Trainspotting (1996) to Spring Breakers (2012). Roeg would go on to perfect this kaleidoscopic approach in Don't Look Now (1973) and The Man Who Fell to Earth (1976), but Performance remains the raw, unfiltered origin point.

sections.content: The film's impact on music-driven cinema can't be overstated. Kenneth Anger's Scorpio Rising (1963) laid groundwork for mixing pop songs with transgressive imagery, but Performance elevated this to feature length. The fusion of John Phillips' score with Mick Jagger's presence created a template followed by Pink Floyd: The Wall (1982) and Under the Cherry Moon (1986). The film's exploration of masculine identity crisis through underworld violence later echoed in Fight Club (1999) and Drive (2011).

Cinematographer Nicolas Roeg's eventual transition to directing marked a new era of British art cinema. His visual innovations - rapid cutting between past/present, extreme close-ups, saturated colors - influenced music video aesthetics and directors like Danny Boyle and Paul Thomas Anderson. The film's blending of reality/fantasy and sexual/criminal underground resurfaced in Naked Lunch (1991) and Only God Forgives (2013). SUBHEAD: Identity and Underground Culture

sections.content: Performance's lasting influence extends beyond technique into themes of identity fluidity. The merging of Chas and Turner predicted contemporary discussions of gender and sexuality, while maintaining a dangerous edge missing from later films. Velvet Goldmine (1998) and I'm Not There (2007) borrowed its rock star metamorphosis ideas, while Sexy Beast (2000) and Legend (2015) echo its London gangster-meets-counterculture clash.
